result.key_differentiator: Plan A delivers a clean, matched event-study design that the firm's stated capability (panel/cohort study, no production ML, no execution infra) can actually build and that a fundamental PM can inspect and challenge end to end, while Plan B piles on IV with a fitted affinity instrument, Driscoll-Kraay/Arellano-Bond/Callaway-Sant'Anna cross-checks and permutation-corrected mechanical regressors that exceed both the team's build capacity and the PM's ability to evaluate credibility.
result.rationale: The question is a mechanism test (does Kalshi cannibalize DraftKings) whose output is meant to move a position in a named stock for a PM who will ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong — this demands a design that is rigorous but fully legible, not maximally sophisticated. Plan A uses matched control groups, cohort/calendar fixed effects, pre-registered functional forms, a proper MDE power gate before running anything, and negative-control placebos (grocery/fuel spend, pseudo-adoption dates, FanDuel-only pipeline) that a fundamental analyst can walk a PM through step by step; the machinery (wild cluster bootstrap, Poisson PML) is invoked only conditionally, and the core estimator is a standard difference-in-differences the audience can sanity-check on an event-time plot. Plan B is more ambitious but overbuilt for this firm: its primary regressor (Kalshi share of wallet) mechanically contains the outcome, forcing an entire permutation-based correction apparatus just to patch a self-inflicted design flaw that Plan A avoids by studying levels directly; its IV strategy requires fitting a user-level 'affinity' score on a holdout sample (edging into the production-ML territory the firm explicitly rules out) and defending an exogeneity story (national non-sports Kalshi volume) that is not obviously valid and would be hard to defend to an IC; and it runs four to five parallel identification strategies (permutation, IV, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Arellano-Bond, out-of-sample refit) that a 3-person data team plus one engineer will struggle to build, maintain, and reconcile within a 6-18 month decision horizon. Plan B's added rigor (wallet-accounting decomposition, take-rate conversion to revenue, FD symmetry check) is genuinely useful and slightly ahead on connecting deposits to economic impact, but the marginal value does not justify the added complexity and reduced legibility for this audience. Given a concentrated single/paired-name bet where a false positive (wrongly shorting DKNG on an illusory substitution effect) is costly and undiversifiable, the tenet that decides this is fit to the firm's evaluative capacity and build capacity, not raw statistical ambition.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B delivers a single, PM-legible cohort/event-time design with a built-in breakdown bound answering 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong,' while Plan A stacks IV, Callaway-Sant'Anna, Arellano-Bond, permutation inference and PPML into a multi-method arbitration scheme that exceeds what a 3-person data team, one engineer, and a fundamental PM can build, execute, or evaluate for conviction.
result.rationale: Both plans attack the same well-posed cannibalization question and both do real work on descriptor hygiene, placebos, pre-trends, and wallet accounting -- this is close. But the firm is a fundamental long/short shop that explicitly can run 'a panel study or a cohort analysis,' has no production-ML build capacity, and needs output a PM can defend by naming what would make it wrong. Plan A reads like it was written for a systematic/quant desk: it layers an instrumented model (affinity x national volume, fit on a holdout, judged by Kleigergen-Paap F-stats) whose exclusion restriction is itself questionable, a staggered-adoption Callaway-Sant'Anna estimator that must be reconciled with the IV result within 2x or deferred to, Arellano-Bond and Driscoll-Kraay corrections, and 1,000-draw permutation inference -- machinery that adds real researcher degrees of freedom and cannot be evaluated by the PM asking naive gut-check questions. It reaches for the sophisticated method before showing the simple one fails, and 'ppmlhdfe leads' is itself a violation of simplest-first for this audience. Plan B keeps one pre-registered primary specification (matched cohort, event-time OLS with user-by-cohort and cohort-by-calendar FE), reports Poisson and other forms as secondary corroboration rather than competing arbiters, and -- crucially -- operationalizes the falsification requirement directly: a partial-identification breakdown value M stating how large the post-trend must be relative to pre-period noise before the confidence set excludes zero, which is exactly the 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' answer a PM can hold in his head. Its matching diagnostics (SMDs, held-out FanDuel and discretionary-spend balance checks) and event-time plot are inspectable early, letting a toxic branch be pruned before the robustness suite is run. Given the concentrated, name-specific use of this output (position sizing on DraftKings), Type I risk is real and both plans build serious defenses against it -- but Plan A's added rigor is diminishing-returns machinery relative to its cost and legibility, whereas Plan B's design is proportionate: rigorous enough to defend a sizing call, simple enough that the team can actually execute and the PM can actually interrogate it.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A answers the question actually asked (ARR on MAU, directly) using panel econometrics the firm is equipped to run, while Plan B reframes the primary claim around seat-growth and builds a ridge-regression nowcast with nested CV and empirical-Bayes shrinkage — closer to the production-ML the firm explicitly will not build.
result.rationale: Both plans are competent and share good instincts: multiple simple baselines, point-in-time data discipline, structural-break screening, consensus-relative scoring, and pre-committed thresholds. The decisive split is firm fit and target fidelity. The mandate says this fund can run panel/cohort studies and buys web/transaction data, but will not build production ML, and needs output a PM can interrogate on a 6-18mo, position-sizing basis. Plan A stays inside classical panel econometrics (fixed effects, unit-root/cointegration diagnostics, clustering/bootstrap SEs) — sophisticated but recognizable machinery for a fundamental shop's quant-adjacent capability, and it regresses log ARR (the actual target) on log MAU directly, exactly the question posed. Its falsification test — refitting on the excluded consumption-metered names and requiring equal performance to sink the thesis — is a genuine negative control derived from the plan's own mechanism, which is exactly the kind of check tenet 9 wants and which Plan B lacks in comparable form. Plan B is intellectually elegant — gating a seat-proxy claim before conditionally building an ARR nowcast is good sequencing in principle — but its secondary stage (pooled fixed-effects ridge, nested-CV tuned penalty, empirical-Bayes shrinkage, Clark-West/DM with HLN correction, 2,000-draw block bootstrap) is a small forecasting-model build that exceeds what a 3-person data team and one engineer at a fundamental L/S shop should be tasked with maintaining, and it drifts the primary claim from ARR to seat-growth, an adjacent quantity, before circling back to ARR only conditionally. That is a real, if partial, goal/target substitution relative to the question as framed. Given breadth here is modest (35-60 names) and the output must be defensible to a PM in plain terms, the more direct, more operationally proportionate design wins.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A gates the whole study behind a bespoke, labor-intensive 'seat-disclosure' dataset (hand-mapping ADP pays-per-control, Paycom clients×employees, Dayforce live customers, Wayback-scraped tier prices, etc.) that a 3-person data team and one engineer cannot realistically build in reasonable time and that yields too thin an N to support the very tight thresholds (β∈[0.5,1.5], partial corr ≥0.45, block-bootstrap significance) it then imposes, whereas Plan B uses a fixed, checkable universe rule (>70% seat-metered revenue) and vendor panels the firm already licenses, reaching a testable, decision-relevant result with a genuine mechanism-derived negative control (consumption-priced names) at comparable rigor and far lower upfront cost.
result.rationale: Both plans are technically excellent and arguably over-instrumented for a fundamental long/short shop's typical audience (Driscoll-Kraay SEs, Clark-West, cointegration tests, wild-cluster bootstraps), so neither wins cleanly on tenet 2's 'audience can evaluate the method' clause — this is a wash. The decisive difference is feasibility and sequencing. Plan A's intellectually appealing mechanism decomposition (MAU→seats→ARR via accounting identity) requires constructing an idiosyncratic 'gate sample' of seat-disclosing companies (payroll/HR names like ADP, Paycom, Dayforce mixed with collaboration-tool names like Atlassian, Asana, Smartsheet) via hand-collected, heterogeneous disclosures and scraped pricing pages. This is exactly the kind of expensive, bespoke data build the tenets caution against committing to before a cheap version has shown the idea is worth pursuing — and it front-loads the most expensive part of the plan rather than the most decisive/cheapest kill test. Worse, the resulting sample is almost certainly too small to support the very demanding statistical thresholds Plan A itself requires (tight beta bounds, partial correlation floors, bootstrap significance, leave-one-out stability), risking a plan that cannot pass its own gate for reasons unrelated to whether the hypothesis is true. Plan B instead defines a clean, rule-based universe (~35-60 names, seat-metered >70% of revenue, standard hostname convention) using data types the firm already buys (web/app panels), reaching ~900-1,000 company-quarters — enough power for the panel methods it proposes — and folds in a real negative control derived from its own mechanism (refitting on excluded consumption-priced names; equal performance sinks the thesis), which is exactly the falsification tenet 9 wants, at no extra data cost. Plan B's benchmarks (naive carry-forward, trailing growth, two-way FE without MAU) are also simpler and more legible to a PM than Plan A's variance-decomposition-plus-ridge-plus-empirical-Bayes pipeline. Plan A's mechanism-first instinct is good practice in principle, but as executed it inverts the 'cheapest, most decisive test first' ordering by making the expensive, hard-to-build piece the prerequisite gate.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B validates actual identification correctness against a held-out ground-truth set with a precision-calibrated abstain rule matched to the stated catastrophic cost of a confident wrong match, while Plan A validates only cluster cohesion and stability and never tests whether a named match is actually correct.
result.rationale: The firm's explicit failure mode is a confident wrong match sizing a position on the wrong bank's customers — this is a Type-I-dominant setting where the burden of proof must fall on precision of the specific ID-to-institution assignment, not on the internal quality of a clustering. Plan A builds an elaborate unsupervised pipeline (Ward/GMM/HDBSCAN ensembles, co-association, PCA) and validates it with silhouette, Calinski-Harabasz, bootstrap Jaccard stability, and cross-window ARI — all of which measure whether clusters are cohesive and reproducible, not whether the eventual name attached to a cluster is correct. Its naming step (Hungarian rank-matching with margin gates) is confirmatory but untested against any ground truth, so a systematic swap between two similar-archetype, similar-size banks in the same country would sail through every gate undetected — precisely the failure mode the PM most fears. Plan B instead treats identification as a calibrated decision problem: it builds a (small but real) labeled validation set (consented survey, provider-revealed seeds, unambiguous public cases), holds out at the institution level (not just customers) via nested leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out CV, and only accepts a match at a pre-committed 95% precision threshold with an explicit abstain sink otherwise. It also runs genuine falsification tests baked into the design — permuted fingerprints must score at chance, phantom IDs must abstain, dropping the largest comparator must degrade gracefully — which directly answers 'what would make this wrong' rather than only reporting internal consistency. B also sequences for information: it pilots the easiest market (concentrated NL) first and pre-commits to stopping if that fails, rather than running the full multi-country pipeline before any go/no-go, and it puts a governance/GDPR gate at the very front, which A never addresses despite working with anonymized personal transaction data — a material omission for a real fund's legal and compliance exposure. Both plans are technically sophisticated and demand real infrastructure, but B pairs its sophistication with a metric (deposit-volume-weighted held-out precision) that is directly interpretable by a PM and directly tied to the risk that matters, whereas A's cluster-quality metrics are one step removed from the actual claim being made.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A builds the false-confident-match risk directly into the design — precision calibrated to 95% via Venn-Abers/conformal, an abstain sink, and validation against real ground-truth labels (consented survey, provider-revealed seeds, unambiguous public cases) — while Plan B's final named-institution step relies only on internal cluster-stability metrics with no comparable external check on whether the name assigned is actually correct.
result.rationale: The PM explicitly named the failure mode that matters: a confident wrong match, because it means sizing a position on the wrong bank's customers. That makes this a Type-I-dominant problem, and the winning plan has to be judged mainly on how well it controls and measures the false-positive rate on the specific deliverable the fund needs — a named, ticker-mapped institution, not a cluster label. Plan A's entire scoring and validation apparatus is built around that: a pre-committed 95%-precision criterion with per-country kill thresholds, an abstain/UNKNOWN sink with explicit reason codes, quarter-versioned anchors to handle bank mergers, leave-one-institution-out and leave-one-country-out nested CV, and — crucially — external ground-truth labels (survey respondents, provider-revealed seeds, unambiguous public cases) used specifically to check whether the named assignment is correct, not just internally consistent. That last piece is what a skeptical PM asking 'what would have to be true for this to be wrong' actually wants to see. Plan B is a genuinely well-sequenced capability build — its country→archetype→name ladder is cheaper to kill early and more tractable for a small data team using standard clustering tools rather than optimal-transport machinery — and its cluster-level validation (bootstrap stability, permutation nulls, four-window ARI) is excellent. But its most important step, named-institution assignment, is validated only by rank-correlation heuristics and internal margin thresholds; there is no external label check on whether the name given is actually right, which is precisely the failure mode the desk cares about. Plan B's honest fallback to 'country and archetype only' is a legitimate scientific answer but does not give the desk what it needs to size a position, whereas Plan A pushes all the way to the deliverable and tells you, per institution, when it doesn't have enough evidence to trust the answer. That direct alignment between the plan's central risk-control mechanism and the PM's stated central fear is the deciding factor.

result.key_differentiator: Plan A requires building a proprietary 40-60 case cross-strata comparables database with a Bayesian likelihood-ratio framework and vendor datasets (DealScan, Infralogic, Bloomberg CACS/DDIS) that a two-analyst desk with no quant staff and no dataset-building capacity cannot construct, evaluate, or maintain, whereas Plan B relies on the primary documents, filings, and expert-network channel checks the firm actually has, sequenced cheapest-kill-first toward a dated, trade-ready verdict.
result.rationale: Both plans correctly frame this as a single-situation mispricing question with a sound H1/H2/H3 taxonomy and pre-registered falsifiers, so tenet 1 is roughly a wash. The split comes on firm fit and sequencing. This desk consumes filings, sell-side, and expert calls; it has no quant research staff and cannot build datasets. Plan A's methodology section is built around coding 40-60 comparable SPV releases across three strata, licensing project-finance and loan databases, and deriving a formal prior with an explicit likelihood-ratio threshold ('20:1-30:1 against H1, ~25x LR needed') - a base rate asserted with false precision before any such database exists, which is invented statistical machinery this audience cannot build or sanity-check, and it front-loads that architecture before the cheap disconfirming checks. Plan B instead leans on the resource this desk actually has - expert-network-style channel checks (counsel, syndicate desk, ex-bankers, OSATs, EDA/IP teams, rival foundry) - uses a small, feasible same-vintage comparable set (5-10 SPVs) rather than a constructed database, explicitly says to check the price reaction first, and states H1 only survives if H2/H3 die via the cheapest disconfirmation. That is exactly the entropy-reducing, adaptive sequencing the framework rewards, and it ends in a trade-sizing step consistent with an event-driven desk whose risk manager cuts positions fast. Plan A's rigor is real but calibrated for a shop with quant infrastructure this platform does not have; Plan B gets to an actionable, inspectable verdict faster using tools this specific desk can actually operate.

Long list of confounders (antitrust, FX review, export control, transfer pricing) risks diffusing focus if not tightly gated by the stated kill criteria

It sequences cheapest disconfirmation first (release language, consent solicitation, EL delta) before the effortful qualification corroboration, and ends with a trade sized to the weakest link — output the PM can act on. Plan B is more statistically rigorous in the abstract, but rigor calibrated to a systematic-signal audience is a defect, not a strength, when the audience is a concentrated single-name book that needs a judgeable verdict on one situation fast.

result.key_differentiator: Plan B checks whether the signal is already sold or arbitraged (vendor landscape scan, McLean-Pontiff decay prior, 2004-2010 replication) and pre-registers a single cheap specification with a 14-day kill gate before committing to any build, whereas Plan A commits to a full domain-adapted transformer pipeline and quarter-scale build before ever asking whether the effect is incremental to what the street and vendors already have.
result.rationale: For a systematic firm whose stated failure modes are crowding, cost, and capacity, the first-order question is not 'can we measure tone precisely' but 'is there anything left to find and can it survive costs' — Plan B attacks that directly with a half-day vendor crowding survey and a literature-grounded prior on decay, then locks a simple LM-based, pre-registered specification with explicit, falsifiable kill criteria (t-threshold, net spread/IR, year and size-quartile consistency, placebo and shuffle tests, vendor rank-correlation as a duplication check) reachable in about two weeks. That is exactly the entropy-reducing, adaptive sequencing the setting calls for: the branch that kills the idea sits at the front, and the expensive infrastructure build (days 11-14, or licensing) is conditional on passing, not sunk regardless of outcome. Plan A is methodologically excellent and well within this firm's ML capability, but it builds the full domain-adapted DeBERTa pipeline, annotation process, and multi-stage validation suite before any cheap check establishes the effect isn't already priced or vendor-sold; LM/FinBERT appear only as an ablation baseline inside a fully built pipeline rather than as the gating first step. It also never asks whether S&P, RavenPack, or Bigdata already sells this, despite crowding being named as this firm's central risk. Both plans use appropriately strict, multiple-testing-aware thresholds suited to a systematic shop that runs many specifications; the difference is Plan B reaches a stop/build decision an order of magnitude faster and cheaper, and that decision is genuinely conditional (pass triggers a build-vs-license comparison, fail triggers a two-page memo naming the likely residual channel), which is what separates a research plan from a task list here.

Plan A takes that at face value, correctly discards management tone as confounded by the negotiation itself, and substitutes a concrete, bottoms-up/top-down spend estimate, contract-mechanics read, vendor-behavior comparables, and a sensitivity table that converts directly into bps of margin and EPS impact — exactly the currency an investment committee needs. Every input (10-K purchase obligations, ASC 350-40/985-20 notes, material contracts exhibits, vendor price lists) is something one analyst can pull from Bloomberg/EDGAR without new infrastructure, and the plan is sequenced so the decisive question (is the dollar exposure even material) comes before the more subtle contract-mechanics and vendor-comparable work — a kill criterion is present and cheap to reach. It also self-corrects for the survivorship problem (bad renewals go unpublicized) by inflating the assumed severity for high-switching-cost customers, and it separates 'immaterial' from 'not uncomfortable,' avoiding false reassurance. This is a plan built for a concentrated, long-horizon, business-risk-focused shop.

Plan B is a well-constructed piece of systematic NLP research — pre-registration, placebo topics, out-of-sample splits, Romano-Wolf corrections, block bootstraps, elastic-net weights, two vendors of transcripts, Visible Alpha/IBES/CRSP/Compustat panels — but almost none of it is something this firm can build, run, or even sanity-check. It also answers a different question: it is a capability-build for a generalizable evasiveness-as-signal factor, not a determination of whether this company's margins are at more risk than guided. Even in its 'success' branch, the deliverable is a cross-sectional predictive score, not a number this PM can put in a model for this position. The publishable-null framing ('H1 true, H2 false is the modal outcome') is honest but underlines that the plan is optimized to learn about a factor, not to resolve the concentrated position in front of the committee this quarter.

It is a single-name deep dive — RPO bridges, tiered haircuts, EV/committed-gross-profit multiples, reverse DCF — that ends in a qualitative constructive/negative verdict on one company's multiple. This is a design a systematic firm can actually operate: replicable, generalizable, and structured to produce a probability-weighted signal rather than a single verdict. Given breadth across markets and a symmetric, diversifiable payoff (a signal deployed across many names), Type II error — killing a real, generalizable effect via an overly demanding single-name bar — is the costlier mistake here, which favors Plan B's design over Plan A's high-threshold single-company gate. But the firm's stated mandate is unusually specific: signals are judged on whether they survive transaction costs, have capacity, and are not already priced/crowded, and are re-run independently by a production research platform. Plan A produces an excellent taxonomy of when LTAs hold versus break (switching-cost/qualification-lag mechanism, strong negative controls in aerospace/LNG vs. MLCC/containers, a genuine out-of-sample holdout on the 2021-2024 auto-semi cycle before trusting the framework, pre-registered falsifiers for the live HBM case) — this is arguably the more rigorously sequenced and better-controlled research design. For a systematic shop, a correct mechanism finding with no linkage to current EV or market-implied duration is not actionable — it identifies truth but not edge. Plan B's core hypothesis is explicitly two-part: the lock-in effect is real, AND current EV does not already price it — and its machinery (RPO bridge, tiered coverage, EV/haircut-adjusted gross profit vs. peers and history, reverse DCF for market-implied horizon) is built to answer exactly that. It is also more naturally suited to the firm's infrastructure: a formulaic, quantifiable pipeline (roll-forward equations, a six-attribute tiering rubric, explicit numeric thresholds for constructive/negative) that a research platform can code and independently rerun, versus Plan A's greater reliance on manual adjudication of litigation records and cross-jurisdiction contract language, which is harder to deterministically replicate at the scale this firm operates. Plan B is not without real flaws — its late-stage threshold list (60%, 40%, 15%, 45%, etc.) reads as calibrated-looking but under-justified precision, and its validation calibrates haircuts and tests them on the same episode set rather than holding out a full cycle the way Plan A does, which is a genuine gap. But the absence of any edge/pricing check in Plan A is more fatal for this specific audience than Plan B's calibration weakness, because a trading firm cannot act on a mechanism finding that never tells it whether the trade is already in the price.
issues_with_winner: Numeric thresholds (60% NTM coverage, 40% year-two, 15% cash support, 45% customer concentration, 50% mirror reconciliation, 2-year horizon gap) are asserted with specific precision but not clearly derived — they read as calibrated when they are largely judgment calls.

No explicit out-of-sample holdout: haircuts are calibrated from prior episodes and then the same episode set is used to 'isolate what distinguished durable cases,' risking in-sample overfitting of the tiering scheme.

High machinery count (six-attribute scoring, three resolution scenarios, 10-15 year depreciation schedule, reverse DCF) adds researcher degrees of freedom that aren't clearly load-bearing relative to a simpler coverage metric.
issues_with_loser: Never reconnects the mechanism finding to current EV or market-implied pricing, so even a fully validated result gives no answer to whether the multiple is justified or already reflects the effect — the stated reason the market cares about this in the first place.

Heavy reliance on manually adjudicated legal/litigation and cross-jurisdiction contract records (PACER, ICC, Delaware Chancery, foreign courts) is hard for an independent team to deterministically re-run at the fidelity the firm's replication culture expects.

Deliberately avoids regression/statistical modeling ('ranked not regressed'), which may be defensible given the bimodal DGP but underuses a quant firm's production ML infrastructure without a clearly stated reason the simple version was tried and failed.
